questions.q: What is the title of the book the Martians discover in the Earth library, and who is its traditional author?
questions.a: The book is *Mother Goose*, a traditional collection of nursery rhymes attributed to the fictional author "Mother Goose". A wrong answer (e.g., "Encyclopaedia Britannica" or "The Art of War") reveals the student has not grasped the central irony: a children's book of nonsense verse defeats a high-tech invasion because the invaders lack cultural context.

questions.q: Why does Think-Tank interpret the rhyme "Humpty Dumpty had a great fall" as a direct threat to himself personally?
questions.a: Think-Tank sees a physical resemblance between himself (large, egg-shaped head, no neck) and Humpty Dumpty (an egg). He interprets "all the King's horses and all the King's men couldn't put Humpty together again" as evidence that Earthlings possess advanced biological warfare capable of destroying a Martian ruler beyond repair. A wrong answer focusing only on "Humpty Dumpty is an egg" misses the personal projection: Think-Tank's narcissism makes him the centre of every threat.

questions.q: If the Martians had read the rhyme "Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water", how might Think-Tank misinterpret "Jack fell down and broke his crown" given his previous pattern of literal reading?
questions.a: Think-Tank would likely interpret "crown" as a royal crown (symbol of leadership) rather than a skull, concluding that Earthlings have developed gravity-based weapons that target rulers specifically. He would cite "Jill came tumbling after" as proof of a coordinated assassination protocol. Steps: 1) Identify the literal meaning of "crown" in the rhyme (head/skull). 2) Recall Think-Tank's pattern: he reads "Mistress Mary's garden" as agriculture, "Humpty" as himself. 3) Apply the pattern: "crown" = royal headgear = threat to monarchy. 4) Predict his reaction: immediate retreat to protect the Martian throne. A wrong answer that gives the *actual* meaning (skull) shows the student cannot adopt the Martian perspective — a key exam skill for this play.

questions.q: Compare the misinterpretations of "Mistress Mary, Quite Contrary" and "Hey Diddle Diddle". How does the *nature* of the perceived threat escalate from the first rhyme to the second?
questions.a: "Mistress Mary" is read as agricultural/chemical warfare ("silver bells and cockle shells" = explosive mines, "pretty maids" = female soldiers). "Hey Diddle Diddle" escalates to *interplanetary* and *technological* threat: the cow jumping over the moon proves Earthlings have mastered space travel and bovine propulsion; the dish running away with the spoon suggests sentient, mobile cutlery — i.e., advanced robotics. The shift is from ground-based bio-chem weapons to space-faring AI. A wrong answer that lists both as "silly mistakes" misses the structural escalation the playwright builds to justify Think-Tank's total panic.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Think-Tank's retreat is a rational decision based on the intelligence available to him." Defend your position using evidence from the play.
questions.a: It is *not* rational. Think-Tank has a crew member (Noodle) who correctly identifies the book as "nursery rhymes — harmless verse for children" and explains the cultural context. Think-Tank dismisses this expert input because of his arrogance ("I am the ruler of Mars... I know better"). A rational leader would weigh the source credibility: Noodle has been right about the book's physical nature (a book, not a sandwich); Think-Tank has been wrong repeatedly (thinking books are sandwiches, then communication devices). The student who calls it "rational" confuses *internal consistency* (Think-Tank follows his own logic) with *objective rationality* (weighing evidence). Board exams reward the distinction.

questions.q: Write a 4-line nursery rhyme about a Martian vegetable (e.g., "Red Radish of Mars") that Think-Tank would misinterpret as a terrifying weapon. Include the misinterpretation he would give.
questions.a:
Example rhyme: "Red Radish of Mars, growing in rows / Emits a bright light wherever it goes / Pull it from soil, hear a pop and a hiss / Earthlings beware of its radioactive kiss."  
Think-Tank's misinterpretation: "A directed-energy root vegetable! 'Pop and a hiss' = sonic boom deployment. 'Radioactive kiss' = nuclear-tipped produce. They weaponise *salads*!"  
A poor answer writes a rhyme but forgets the *misinterpretation*, or writes a misinterpretation that doesn't follow Think-Tank's established pattern (literal, military, self-referential). This tests whether the student has internalised the *mechanism* of the comedy.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: This topic covers the climax and resolution of the play where the Martians, led by Think-Tank, discover a book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes in a 20th-century library and ______ the literal imagery (e.g., "Humpty Dumpty had a great fall" as a threat of biological warfare, "Hey Diddle Diddle" as evidence of advanced Earthling space technology) as proof of Earth's superior military and scientific capabilities, causing them to abort their invasion and flee Mars.

Fill in the blank: This topic covers the climax and resolution of the play where the Martians, led by Think-Tank, discover a book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes in a ______th-century library and misinterpret the literal imagery (e.g., "Humpty Dumpty had a great fall" as a threat of biological warfare, "Hey Diddle Diddle" as evidence of advanced Earthling space technology) as proof of Earth's superior military and scientific capabilities, causing them to abort their invasion and flee Mars.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to explain, with textual evidence, how at least three specific nursery rhymes are misinterpreted by Think-Tank and his crew, and trace how each misinterpretation escalates Think-Tank's fear until he orders the evacuation of Mars.
